stem: Cover the underlined sentence. What job does it do in the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a memoir by a nutrition researcher.

For years my mother weighed every portion on a kitchen scale and wrote its calories in a green notebook. My father, by contrast, cooked by smell and stopped eating when the dinner conversation ran out. <u>She trusted numbers; he trusted his appetite.</u> I grew up to study the science of feeling full, which may be my way of trying to settle their argument.
choices: It sums up the difference between the two parents described before it.
It shows that the parents often argued aloud about how much to eat.
It suggests that the father had no interest in his own health.
It introduces the narrator's later career in nutrition research.
explanation: Read the sentences on either side. The two before it describe the mother's scale and notebook and the father's cooking by smell. The underlined line compresses both into six words, so its job is to sum up the contrast you have just read. This is the move behind the real question about the function of an underlined line in fiction or memoir: name what the line does next to its neighbours, not just what it says.

B.why: You took 'settle their argument' in the last sentence literally and invented a spoken quarrel. The text never shows the parents arguing. 'Argument' means their opposite views, not a fight. Before you pick a choice, find the words that support it.

C.why: You read 'trusted his appetite' as not caring about health. The text says only how he decided when to stop eating. It says nothing about how he felt about his health, so this choice adds something the text doesn't contain.

D.why: You gave the job of the next sentence to the underlined one. The narrator's career comes in the final sentence. The underlined line looks back at the parents, not forward to the career.

stem: Cover the underlined sentence. What job does it do in the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel.

Ines had counted the frogs in the marsh every spring for eleven years, and each year the count was smaller. This April she walked the whole shore and heard nothing but wind. <u>The silence followed her home and sat down with her at the kitchen table.</u> She did not open her field notebook that night.
choices: It conveys how the empty marsh continues to weigh on Ines at home.
It indicates that Ines's house was unusually quiet that evening.
It explains why the frogs in the marsh had declined over the years.
It describes the route Ines took as she walked around the marsh.
explanation: Silence can't really follow anyone or sit at a table. The image is figurative. The sentence before it gives the silent marsh, and the sentence after shows Ines too low to open her notebook. So the line shows the loss staying with her after she leaves the shore. Reading an image for its feeling rather than as a physical fact is the key step in questions about the function of an underlined literary line.

B.why: You read the image as a physical fact. The 'silence' is the missing frog calls from the marsh, not a quiet house. The literal reading doesn't fit the sentences around it, which are about the frogs, not her home.

C.why: The text says the frogs declined but never says why. Can you point to any words that give a cause? You can't, so this choice invents content.

D.why: You attached the underlined line to the earlier sentence about walking the shore. The underlined line takes place after she has gone home. It says nothing about her route.

stem: Cover the underlined sentence. What job does it do in the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a memoir by a music historian.

Among my grandfather's belongings was a hand-copied book of fiddle tunes, its pages gone soft from use. <u>For him it was less a songbook than a map back to the village he had left at nineteen.</u> He played from it every Sunday, though he had long since memorized every tune in it.
choices: It shows that the book mattered to him for more than its music.
It indicates that the book held directions to his home village.
It reveals that he regretted leaving his village at nineteen.
It describes the worn condition of the book's handwritten pages.
explanation: The line says the book was 'less a songbook than a map back' to his village. That means it carried his memory of home. The next sentence backs this up: he already knew every tune, so he didn't open it for the notes. The line's job is to show that an object means more than its practical use. Questions about the function of an underlined line often hinge on exactly this kind of meaning.

B.why: You took 'map' literally. The book is a book of fiddle tunes, and the sentence calls it a map only in a figurative sense. Reading it as real directions clashes with everything else the text says about it.

C.why: The text says he left at nineteen and stayed attached to the village. It never says he regretted leaving. Missing a place and wishing you had stayed are different things, and this choice adds the second.

D.why: The soft, worn pages come from the first sentence. You described a detail next to the underlined line instead of what the line itself does.

stem: Cover the underlined sentence. What job does it do in the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel.

The surveyors who came before Tomas had drawn the coastline as a single smooth, confident curve. <u>Tomas walked it instead, a mile a day, marking every inlet and every fallen rock.</u> His employers, who had expected a finished map within one season, received it four years later.
choices: It sets Tomas's careful method against the approach of earlier surveyors.
It suggests that Tomas disliked the surveyors who had worked before him.
It lists the measuring instruments Tomas carried along the coastline.
It explains how Tomas's employers reacted to his finished map.
explanation: The sentence before it gives the earlier surveyors' quick, smooth curve. The word 'instead' then signals that Tomas did the opposite: slow, mile-by-mile, every detail. The line's job is to show how Tomas differs from them. Spotting a character contrast from the line next door is one of the most common jobs in questions about the function of an underlined line in fiction.

B.why: Working differently from someone doesn't mean disliking them. The text shows a contrast in method and says nothing about Tomas's feelings toward the other surveyors, so this choice invents an attitude.

C.why: No instruments appear anywhere in the text. Tomas marks inlets and rocks, but you can't point to any words naming a tool, so this list is made up.

D.why: The employers and the four-year wait come in the next sentence. You gave the job of the following line to the underlined one, which is only about how Tomas worked.
